title: Glass Plates and a World on Camera
summary: In 1851 photographers started making pictures on sheets of glass coated with a sticky goo that had to stay wet. Suddenly photos were sharp, cheap and quick, and cameras went everywhere: to battlefields, up in balloons and deep into the mountains of California.

sections.heading: A Sticky Liquid That Changed Everything
paragraphs: By 1850, photography had a split personality. The daguerreotype was dazzlingly sharp, but every picture was a one-off on a silver mirror that could never be copied. Talbot's calotype could make many prints from one paper negative, but the fibres of the paper made everything look slightly fuzzy, as if seen through a fog. Photographers wanted the best of both: the sharpness of a mirror and the copying power of a negative. The answer turned out to be a material that was already lying around in every home: glass.

Glass is clear, smooth and flat, which makes it a perfect base for a negative. The problem was getting light-sensitive silver to stick to it. Silver salts will not cling to bare glass any more than paint sticks to a greasy window. You need a thin, clear 'glue' to hold them in place. Several inventors had tried egg white. Then an English sculptor and chemist named Frederick Scott Archer tried something stranger.

Collodion is a syrupy liquid made by dissolving guncotton (cotton treated with nitric and sulfuric acids) in a mixture of ether and alcohol. Doctors used it as a kind of liquid bandage, because when it is painted onto skin the ether and alcohol evaporate and leave a tough, transparent film. Archer had been experimenting since about 1848, and in March 1851 he published his method in a magazine called The Chemist. It became known as the wet collodion process, or simply the wet plate.

Here is what a photographer actually had to do, step by step. First, clean a sheet of glass until it squeaks. Second, pour a pool of collodion, mixed with a little iodide or bromide salt, onto the middle of the plate and tilt it carefully so the syrup flows to every corner in an even layer, then pour the extra back into the bottle. Third, in a darkened room, lower the sticky plate into a bath of silver nitrate solution for a few minutes. The silver joins with the iodide and bromide to form light-sensitive silver halide crystals trapped inside the collodion skin. Fourth, slide the plate, still dripping, into a light-tight holder, rush to the camera and take the picture. Fifth, hurry back to the dark and pour developer over the plate so the hidden image appears. Finally, fix it, wash it and varnish it to protect it.

The catch is in the name: wet. The plate only stayed sensitive while the collodion was moist. Once it dried, the silver bath crystallised, the chemicals stopped working properly and the picture was ruined. From the moment the plate was coated to the moment it was developed, a photographer usually had only about 10 to 15 minutes. On a hot, dry day it could be even less. Every single photograph was a small race against the clock.

Why put up with such a fuss? Because the results were spectacular. A glass negative was crystal clear, so prints made from it were razor sharp, with fine detail in faces, leaves and brickwork. It could be printed again and again, usually onto paper coated with egg white and silver called albumen paper. And it was fast. In good daylight an exposure took just a few seconds, compared with half a minute or more for many earlier methods. For portraits, that was the difference between a stiff, frozen expression and something closer to a natural face.

Most generous of all, Archer chose not to patent his invention. Anyone could use it for free. Within a few years the wet plate had swept across the world and, by the end of the 1860s, it had almost completely replaced the daguerreotype. Sadly, Archer earned very little from his gift. He died in London in 1857, still in his early forties, in poor health and poor circumstances. Fellow photographers raised money for his family, and a small government pension later helped support his children.

The wet plate had one more odd habit that you can still see in old photographs. Its silver crystals reacted strongly to blue and ultraviolet light but hardly at all to red, orange or yellow, and only weakly to green. So a blue sky, full of blue light, turned completely black on the negative and printed as blank white. Clouds vanished. Red lips and rosy cheeks, which send back little blue light, came out dark, and a ripe tomato could look like a shiny black ball.

sections.heading: Pictures for Pennies: Ambrotypes, Tintypes and Cartes de Visite
paragraphs: The wet plate did not only make better negatives. With a clever twist, it could also make cheap pictures that needed no printing at all. If a collodion negative on glass is slightly underexposed and then laid against something black, a strange thing happens. The thin, silvery parts of the image reflect light and look pale, while the clear glass shows the black backing and looks dark. Your eye reads the negative as a positive picture.

This was the ambrotype. James Ambrose Cutting of Boston took out several patents on versions of it in 1854, and the name, from Greek words meaning something like 'immortal impression', may have been invented in the Philadelphia studio of a daguerreotypist named Marcus Aurelius Root. Photographers backed the glass with black velvet, black varnish or dark red glass, then set it in a little folding case lined with velvet, just like a daguerreotype. Ambrotypes were much cheaper than daguerreotypes and did not have that confusing mirror shine, so by the late 1850s they had become more popular.

Then came something even cheaper and tougher. Instead of glass, why not use a thin sheet of iron painted black? The image would sit on the dark surface and appear as a positive, just like an ambrotype, but it would not shatter if dropped. Adolphe-Alexandre Martin described the idea in Paris in 1853, and Hamilton Smith patented it in the United States in 1856. It went by several names, including melainotype and ferrotype, but the one that stuck was tintype, even though there was no tin in it at all.

Tintypes were the fast food of photography. Because there was no drying and no printing, a customer could sit for a picture and walk away with it a few minutes later. Travelling photographers set up tents at fairs, beaches and carnivals. Soldiers in the American Civil War tucked tintypes of themselves into letters home, and carried pictures of sweethearts and children in their pockets, where a glass picture would have cracked. Sizes ranged from tiny 'gem' portraits small enough for a locket up to large plates, and tintypes stayed popular as a seaside and fairground novelty well into the 1900s. Some artists still make them today.

Meanwhile in Paris, a photographer called André-Adolphe-Eugène Disdéri had a money-saving idea. In 1854 he patented a way to take several small portraits on one glass negative, by using a camera with multiple lenses or a back that slid across between exposures. One plate and one printing gave a whole sheet of little pictures, which were cut apart and glued onto stiff cards about the size of a modern business card, roughly 6 by 10 centimetres. They were called cartes de visite, French for 'visiting cards'.

For a few years the idea was only moderately successful. Then in 1859 Disdéri published small portraits of Emperor Napoleon III, and suddenly everyone wanted one. He charged 20 francs for a dozen pictures, at a time when one large portrait print could cost 50 to 100 francs. The craze, nicknamed 'cardomania', spread across Europe and America in the 1860s. People swapped cards with friends and visitors, and collected cards of queens, generals, actors and authors, which photographers sold in shop windows. In the United States alone, an estimated 300 to 400 million cartes de visite were sold each year during the 1860s.

To hold all these cards, families bought thick photograph albums with cut-out windows on each page. The album sat in the front parlour, and showing it to guests became part of a visit. Many historians compare it to an early form of social media: a public display of who you knew, who you admired and how you wanted to look. For the first time in history, an ordinary clerk or shopkeeper could own pictures of grandparents, cousins and children, as well as the face of the queen.

sections.heading: A Darkroom on Wheels: Roger Fenton in the Crimea
paragraphs: The wet plate created a puzzle for any photographer who wanted to leave the studio. If every plate had to be coated, exposed and developed within a quarter of an hour, then the darkroom had to come too. Landscape photographers loaded mules, carts and boats with tents, glass, bottles of chemicals, water tanks, heavy wooden cameras and tripods. In the field, a photographer would crawl inside a light-tight tent or wagon, coat a plate by the dim glow of yellow or orange glass, run out to the camera, then rush back in to develop it.

The most famous early example was a British photographer named Roger Fenton. In 1854 Britain, France and the Ottoman Empire went to war with Russia on the Crimean peninsula, on the northern shore of the Black Sea. Newspaper reports about the suffering of British soldiers in the cold and mud had shocked people at home. Encouraged by Prince Albert and the government's Secretary of State for War, and paid for by the print publisher Thomas Agnew and Sons, Fenton set out to photograph the war.

He sailed in February 1855 and landed at the harbour of Balaklava on 8 March. With him came an assistant, Marcus Sparling, a servant named William, and a large horse-drawn van, said to have once belonged to a wine merchant, rebuilt as a travelling darkroom. Around it were piled hundreds of glass plates and chests of chemicals.

Working conditions were awful. As spring turned into summer, the heat inside the dark van became stifling, so hot that the collodion sometimes dried almost as soon as it was poured. Dust stuck to the sticky plates. Fenton fell and broke several ribs, and later caught cholera. He was also deeply upset by the misery he saw around him.

Fenton could not photograph actual fighting. His exposures took several seconds and his equipment was enormous, so anything moving fast simply turned into a blur, and setting up near the battle lines would have been both impossible and deadly. Instead he photographed what could stand still: officers and soldiers posing in groups, camps and cooking huts, the crowded harbour, and the bare, rocky landscape. He also chose not to photograph dead or wounded soldiers, partly because his pictures were meant to be sold to the public and partly, perhaps, to avoid upsetting families at home.

His most famous image shows a stony road winding through an empty valley, scattered with cannonballs. Agnew exhibited it in London in September 1855 with the title The Valley of the Shadow of Death, borrowed from the Bible. There are actually two versions, one with cannonballs on the road and one without, and for many years people argued about whether Fenton moved the cannonballs to make the scene more dramatic. In 2007 the filmmaker Errol Morris studied the shadows and pebbles carefully and concluded that the empty-road picture was taken first. That means someone probably placed the cannonballs on the road for the second shot. Even the first great war photograph may have been arranged.

Fenton stayed in the Crimea until 22 June 1855 and came home with more than 350 usable large negatives. An exhibition of over 300 prints toured London and other British cities, and he showed them to Queen Victoria, Prince Albert and the French Emperor Napoleon III. Sales were disappointing, but the idea was now planted: a camera could follow an army and show people at home what war looked like, at least when it was standing still.

sections.heading: Brady's Teams and the American Civil War
paragraphs: Six years after Fenton came home, a much bigger and bloodier war broke out across the Atlantic. The American Civil War (1861–1865) was the first major war to be photographed on a large scale, and the name most connected with it is Mathew Brady. Brady was already America's most famous portrait photographer. He had opened a studio in New York in 1844 and another in Washington, D.C., in 1849, and he had photographed presidents, senators and celebrities. On the day in 1860 when Abraham Lincoln gave an important speech at the Cooper Union in New York, he also sat for a portrait in Brady's studio.

When the war began, Brady decided to create a complete photographic record of it, at his own expense. But here is something many people do not realise: Brady himself took very few of the war photographs. His eyesight had been getting worse since the 1850s, and he worked more like a director or publisher. He hired and equipped teams of photographers, around twenty of them, each with a travelling darkroom wagon, and sent them to follow the armies. Among them were Alexander Gardner, a Scottish-born photographer who had managed Brady's Washington studio, Timothy O'Sullivan, who had started out as a teenage apprentice in Brady's studio, and George Barnard.

The pictures were published under the label 'Brady' even when someone else had taken them, which was normal business practice then but frustrated the men in the field. By 1863 Gardner had left to open his own studio in Washington, and O'Sullivan and others went to work with him.

The war wagons became a familiar sight. Soldiers, seeing the strange black-covered carts with chemical smells drifting out, sometimes called them 'What-is-it? wagons'. Inside, photographers worked in heat, dust and danger. Like Fenton, they could not capture battles while they were happening. Exposures still took seconds, and gunsmoke, galloping horses and running men would have been nothing but blurs. What they could photograph was what came before and after: camps, cannons, bridges, ruined towns, generals in front of their tents, and the battlefield once the fighting had stopped.

sections.heading: The Dead of Antietam
paragraphs: On 17 September 1862, near Antietam Creek and the small town of Sharpsburg, Maryland, Union and Confederate armies fought the bloodiest single day in American history. About 23,000 soldiers were killed, wounded, captured or missing in a single day. Within a day or two, Alexander Gardner and his assistant James Gibson arrived with their wagon and cameras. Over the next few days they photographed the battlefield while many of the fallen soldiers had not yet been buried.

This was something completely new. According to historians, it was the first time an American battlefield had been photographed before the dead were taken away. Many of Gardner's pictures were made as stereographs, pairs of photographs that look three-dimensional in a special viewer, which made the scenes feel even more real and close.

In October 1862, Brady put the photographs on display at his gallery on Broadway in New York, under the title The Dead of Antietam. Until then, most civilians in Northern cities knew the war through newspaper reports, printed lists of names, drawings in magazines, and letters from soldiers. Paintings and engravings of battles usually showed brave charges, flags and heroic poses. Now crowds stood in a city gallery looking quietly at real photographs of a road, a fence, a field, and the soldiers who had died there.

Visitors were deeply moved. Some leaned in with magnifying glasses to study the faces, afraid they might recognise someone they knew. The New York Times wrote that Brady had done something to bring home to the public 'the terrible reality and earnestness of war', and added that if he had not brought the bodies and laid them in people's dooryards and along their streets, he had 'done something very like it'. A photograph, people realised, could make faraway events feel close in a way that words could not.

For Brady, the war ended in money trouble. He had spent more than 100,000 dollars making over 10,000 plates, expecting the government to buy the collection. It did not, at least not for years, and he went bankrupt. Congress finally paid him 25,000 dollars in 1875, but he died in poverty in 1896. Today the Library of Congress and the National Archives hold thousands of these glass negatives, and they remain one of the most important visual records of the war.

sections.heading: Above the Rooftops: Nadar and the First Aerial Photographs
paragraphs: While some photographers headed to war, a Parisian with flaming red hair headed straight up. His real name was Gaspard-Félix Tournachon, but everyone knew him as Nadar. He began as a caricaturist, drawing funny pictures of famous people for humour magazines, and he moved into photography in the 1850s. By 1860 he had a grand studio at 35 Boulevard des Capucines in Paris, with his name written in giant letters across the front.

Nadar's portraits were very different from the stiff, fussy pictures of many studios. He used soft natural daylight from big windows, a plain background, and simple poses, and he chatted with his sitters to bring out their personalities. His camera recorded many of the most famous people in France: the novelist Victor Hugo, the poet Charles Baudelaire, the composer Franz Liszt and the actress Sarah Bernhardt.

Nadar also loved balloons. In 1858 he rose above Paris in a tethered balloon and made what are considered the first aerial photographs. Picture the problem: he had to coat, expose and develop wet plates inside a swaying wicker basket, with his darkroom crammed in alongside him, while the gas from the balloon could spoil his chemicals. Those very first photographs no longer survive. Later, he built a huge balloon called Le Géant ('The Giant') in 1863, and he experimented with taking photographs underground in the Paris catacombs using artificial electric light. During the siege of Paris in 1870–71, he helped organise balloon flights that carried letters out of the surrounded city, often described as the world's first airmail service.

The oldest aerial photograph that still exists was taken on the other side of the Atlantic. On 13 October 1860, the photographer James Wallace Black and the balloonist Samuel Archer King went up over Boston in a balloon called the Queen of the Air and photographed the city from several hundred metres up (accounts give heights from about 370 to 630 metres). The picture shows a crowded patchwork of rooftops, church spires, streets and ships' masts. Black gave it a poetic title: Boston, as the Eagle and the Wild Goose See It. For the first time, people could see their own town the way only birds ever had.

sections.heading: Art, Fame and 3D: Julia Margaret Cameron and the Stereoscope
paragraphs: Was photography an art, or just a machine for copying? Victorians argued about this endlessly, and one woman answered with her camera. Julia Margaret Cameron was born in Calcutta, India, in 1815, and lived much of her later life at Freshwater on the Isle of Wight, in a house called Dimbola. Around Christmas 1863, when she was about 48 years old, her daughter and son-in-law gave her a camera. It changed her life.

Cameron turned her coal house into a darkroom and a glass-roofed chicken house into a studio, which she called her 'glass house'. Then she persuaded, and sometimes practically ordered, family members, servants, neighbours and famous visitors to sit for her. Her neighbour was the poet Alfred Tennyson. Other sitters included the scientists Charles Darwin and John Herschel, the very man who had helped invent photographic fixing, and the young actress Ellen Terry.

Her pictures looked unlike anyone else's. She came in very close, filling the frame with a face. She used dramatic light from one side, dark backgrounds and long exposures, and she often let the image go slightly out of focus on purpose. Some of her plates show smudges, scratches and swirls in the collodion. Many critics hated this. One 1865 review complained that her blurry effects came at the expense of all the other qualities of a good photograph. But Cameron was not trying to make a perfect record. She wanted to capture something of a person's character and mood, the way a painter might. In about twelve years she made roughly 900 photographs, and today she is seen as one of the great artists of early photography.

Meanwhile, in many middle-class homes, people were enjoying photography as a kind of magic show. The stereoscope used a simple trick of human vision. Because your two eyes are a few centimetres apart, each sees the world from a slightly different angle, and your brain combines the two views to judge depth. In 1838 the scientist Charles Wheatstone showed that if each eye is shown a separate drawing made from a slightly different viewpoint, the brain fuses them into a single solid-looking scene.

Photography made this easy. A stereo camera with two lenses, side by side, took two pictures at once, which were mounted next to each other on a card. In 1849 David Brewster suggested a viewer using lenses, small enough to hold in your hands. When Queen Victoria admired stereoscopes at the Great Exhibition in London in 1851, a craze began. Later, in 1861, the American writer and doctor Oliver Wendell Holmes designed a cheap, simple viewer with two lenses, a wooden hood and a stand for the card. He deliberately did not patent it, and versions of it were made for about a century.

Families could now sit by the fire and 'visit' the pyramids of Egypt, the streets of Paris, Niagara Falls or the battlefields of the Civil War in startling depth. Companies sold boxed sets of stereo cards like we might buy box sets of shows. It was, in a way, the virtual reality of the Victorian age.

sections.heading: Mountains That Persuaded a Nation
paragraphs: The wet plate also travelled into wild places, and some of those pictures helped protect the land itself. Carleton Watkins was a photographer in San Francisco who, in July 1861, made a journey into Yosemite Valley in the Sierra Nevada mountains of California. Most Americans in the East had never seen it, and many found written descriptions of granite cliffs and giant waterfalls hard to believe.

Watkins carried an enormous camera that used 'mammoth plates', glass negatives roughly 46 by 56 centimetres (about 18 by 22 inches). With no easy way to enlarge prints, a big picture needed a big negative, and each huge sheet had to be coated and developed on the spot. Along with the glass, he brought a stereo camera, chemicals and a darkroom tent, carried on pack animals over rough trails.

The results were breathtaking: sheer walls of El Capitan, Yosemite Falls dropping down the cliffs, giant sequoia trees and calm rivers reflecting the mountains like mirrors. Watkins became famous for these reflection pictures. His prints were shown in New York and Washington, and California's senator John Conness made sure members of Congress saw them.

In 1864, in the middle of the Civil War, Congress passed and President Abraham Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant, which set aside Yosemite Valley and the Mariposa Grove of giant sequoias to be protected 'for public use, resort and recreation'. It was the first time the US government set aside land especially to protect its natural beauty, and it paved the way for the national parks that followed. Many historians believe Watkins's photographs helped persuade lawmakers that the place was worth saving.

Watkins himself had a sad ending. Rivals copied his pictures without credit, which the law did not prevent at the time; he lost his business through debts; and much of his work was destroyed in the San Francisco earthquake and fire of 1906. He died in 1916 in a state hospital. But the valley he photographed is still protected today.

By 1880 the camera had been carried into wars, up into the sky, onto mountaintops and into millions of parlour albums. Yet one thing still defeated every photographer on Earth. Anything that moved quickly, a running child, a flying bird, the legs of a galloping horse, came out as a ghostly smear. The dream was clear: to freeze a split second so perfectly that you could see what the human eye was too slow to notice. Could anyone ever photograph a horse at full gallop without a blur?

deepDive: Why did the wet collodion process dominate photography for about thirty years despite its awkwardness? The answer lies in a trade-off between sensitivity, sharpness and reproducibility. A calotype paper negative scattered light through its fibres, softening every print. A daguerreotype was sharp but unique. Collodion on glass offered a smooth, transparent, grainless base, so an albumen print made by contact (laying the negative directly on paper in sunlight) could reproduce extremely fine detail. Its sensitivity was also much higher, partly because the silver halide was developed while the plate was still wet and chemically active. Exposures fell from minutes to a few seconds in daylight, which made the carte de visite trade, mass-produced stereographs and fieldwork possible. The drawbacks were serious. Ether and alcohol fumes were unpleasant and flammable, and some photographers suffered from the chemicals, including the poisonous potassium cyanide sometimes used as a fixer. The emulsion responded mainly to blue and ultraviolet light (it was 'colour-blind' to red and only weakly sensitive to green), so skies printed white and red objects dark. Historians also debate how 'truthful' these images were. Fenton's two versions of The Valley of the Shadow of Death, and evidence that a body was moved for a Gardner photograph at Gettysburg in 1863, show that staging began almost as soon as war photography itself. Another debate is about credit. Brady's name appears on thousands of images actually made by Gardner, O'Sullivan, Barnard and others, so modern archives try to identify the true photographer whenever possible. The influence of photography on policy is also discussed cautiously: Watkins's pictures were circulated in Congress before the 1864 Yosemite Grant, but the law also came from lobbying by Californians who wanted the valley protected, so photographs were one powerful argument among several, not the only cause. Finally, the economics matter. Archer gave his process away freely, while Talbot had tried to enforce patents on paper negatives. The open, unpatented wet plate spread rapidly, a useful early lesson in how sharing an invention can speed up its adoption.
funFact: The oldest surviving aerial photograph, taken over Boston from a balloon in 1860, was titled Boston, as the Eagle and the Wild Goose See It.
